analysis.one_liner: Requires federal contractors and federal agencies to pay workers enough to lift a family of four out of poverty.
analysis.headline: The bill to require a living wage for federal contract workers — backed by 65 House Democrats — was never taken up by either committee and died without a single vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the federal government and companies with federal contracts over $10,000 to pay every worker enough that a 40-hour week lifts a family of four above the federal poverty line, plus extra pay to cover benefits the employer does not provide. Employers that repeatedly violate the wage rule could lose their federal contracts and be barred from new ones for five years, and workers could sue for back pay and damages. Small businesses and nonprofits with modest pay gaps between CEOs and lowest-paid workers would be exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal contract workers and federal employees who are paid below the poverty level for a family of four. According to the bill's findings, about 162,000 of the 1.4 million federal contract workers earned less than that amount in fiscal 1999, and 14,356 federal government employees did as of September 2000. The bill's findings note a majority of these workers are adult women working full-time, with a disproportionate share minorities. Workers would also gain protection from being fired for complaining about their pay, and could recover triple damages if an employer willfully shorted them.

how_it_helps.text: Would require the federal government and any employer with a federal contract over $10,000 to pay each worker an hourly wage sufficient to earn the federal poverty level for a family of four in a 40-hour week, plus a locality-based top-up to cover fringe benefits the employer does not provide.

Would cover roughly 162,000 of 1.4 million federal contract workers who, per the bill's findings, earned below that poverty level in fiscal 1999 — just under 60% of them at large firms and 62% on Department of Defense contracts — plus 14,356 federal employees who earned less than that amount as of September 2000.
Would make it illegal to fire or suspend a worker for alleging a wage violation, and give workers a private right of action with back pay, attorney fees, and triple damages for willful violations.

Would let the Labor Secretary cancel contracts and bar from new federal contracts for five years any contractor engaged in a pattern of violating the wage requirement, and hold it liable for the government's cost of finding a replacement.
Would exempt small businesses entirely, and exempt nonprofits unless their CEO-to-lowest-worker pay ratio exceeded 25 to 1, so the mandate would fall mainly on large contractors.

analysis.who_pays: Large federal contractors — especially defense firms — would pay higher wages and benefit costs, and would face contract cancellation and a five-year debarment for repeat violations. The federal government itself would pay more to bring its own 14,356 below-poverty workers up to the living wage, and some of the added contractor cost would likely be passed on to taxpayers through contract prices. Small businesses and qualifying nonprofits would be exempt from the mandate.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large federal contractors and federal agencies

drawbacks.text: The added wages and benefit top-ups would raise the cost of federal contracts, and a portion of that would likely be passed on to taxpayers through higher contract prices.

The wage floor is keyed to the poverty line for a family of four regardless of a worker's household size, so it pays the same minimum to a single worker as to a sole breadwinner with children, and the locality-based fringe-benefit top-up would require a new system of Labor Department rules to administer.

Because small businesses are fully exempt, the mandate could shift contracting work toward smaller firms and make it harder for the government to compare bids on equal footing, while the safe harbor lets contractors escape debarment simply by entering a consent agreement and paying back wages.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — moving about 176,000 federal and contract workers above the poverty line, with real enforcement teeth and protection against retaliation — is substantial and targeted at workers whose low pay is effectively subsidized by federal dollars. The costs are real but bounded: small businesses and most nonprofits are exempt, the President could suspend the mandate in an emergency, and contractors with repeated violations could avoid debarment by paying back wages under a consent agreement. The main design weakness is the bluntness of a single family-of-four wage floor and the untested fringe-benefit top-up, but on balance the bill's costs fall on the large contractors that profit from the current arrangement.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in two House committees and their subcommittees for the rest of the Congress and was never reported out, debated, or voted on.

narrative.text: Rep. Luis Gutierrez introduced the Federal Living Wage Responsibility Act on April 4, 2001, with 65 cosponsors, all Democrats.

The Speaker referred it to two committees — Government Reform and Education and the Workforce — each 'for consideration of such provisions as fall within its jurisdiction,' splitting the bill's fate across two panels at the outset.

Within three months it had been sent down to three subcommittees: Technology and Procurement Policy in April 2001, and Employer-Employee Relations and Workforce Protections in June 2001. No markup, report, or floor action ever followed.
The 107th Congress ended January 3, 2003 with the bill still in committee, so it expired with no vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large federal contractors — the big firms, particularly on Defense Department contracts, whose workers were being paid below the poverty line — came out ahead, since they never had to raise wages or face debarment. The House Republican majority that controlled committee scheduling also got the outcome it preferred: the bill never reached the floor.

for.name: Rep. Luis Gutierrez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Federal Living Wage Responsibility Act and recruited 65 cosponsors.

for.name: 65 of 208 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including members such as George Miller, Nancy Pelosi, John Conyers, and Maxine Waters.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling committee scheduling and the House floor
against.what_they_did: Held 223 of 432 House seats, chaired both committees of referral and all three subcommittees it was sent to, and never scheduled a markup or floor vote; the bill died in committee.

against.name: Federal contractor industry
against.role: Large firms holding the $208 billion in annual federal contracts cited in the bill
against.what_they_did: Would have borne the wage mandate and debarment penalties; the bill's own findings note just under 60% of underpaid contract workers were at large firms.

sides.party_line_note: All 65 cosponsors were Democrats and none of the 223 House Republicans supported it; the bill never reached a roll-call vote, so no floor votes exist to confirm the split.

industries.note: The bill would have forced large contractors to pay roughly 162,000 underpaid workers a poverty-line wage plus benefit top-ups, and exposed repeat violators to cancellation and five-year debarment. Its own findings show these workers are concentrated at large firms and on Defense Department contracts.
Both categories are fully exempt, so the bill would have given them a cost advantage over large contractors bidding for federal work.
The government itself would have had to raise pay for the 14,356 federal employees earning below the family-of-four poverty level, at direct cost to the Treasury.
